A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DSR-Bench with the same authors, core data structures, operations, and synthetic instances. Both complete documents, including appendices, are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine LLMs, prompting comparisons, spatial and natural-language experiments, and detailed appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations, expands coverage to ten LLMs, and adds code-generation experiments and diagnostic studies.

M1.justification: The canonical benchmark retains its data-structure operations, synthetic generation, structured answers, and exact-match scoring. No new trained model or proposed reasoning algorithm is introduced; the code-generation modes and strategy-selection studies are evaluation interventions.

E1.justification: The existing main, challenge, spatial, and natural-language coverage remains. v2 adds code-generation and interpreter-use scenarios across seven existing structures. Appendix A.13 also evaluates new task requirements: selecting BFS versus DFS for graph problems and choosing arrays versus K-D trees for nearest-neighbor queries.

E2.justification: GPT-5 joins the main and challenge comparisons. The new code experiments compare Default, CodeMaybe, CodeEnforce, and CodeOnly across six models, substantially expanding the evaluated response-method comparisons. The original five prompting strategies remain.

E3.justification: v2 specifies GPT-5 with medium thinking effort and replaces Gemini-2.5-Pro-Preview-03-25 with the stable version. New protocols distinguish externally executed Python from internal code simulation, compare API and ChatGPT web execution, test five prompt paraphrases, and evaluate strategy selection on ten-case sets. Core length ranges and binary scoring remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds code-mode and web-interface ablations, a CoT reasoning-format comparison, JSON-parsing validation, formal-template paraphrase tests, and strategy-adaptation studies. It also adds reasoning-trace inspection and quantitative analysis of K-D-tree median, tie-breaking, and axis errors. The Levenshtein analysis already exists in v1 and is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run evaluations, appendix means and standard deviations, and Figure 2 error bars. v2 uses the existing three-run practice for additional evaluations; no new seed policy, confidence-interval procedure, or significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 results, including 0.79 overall in Table 1 and a reported 0.498 challenge score. Gemini's overall score changes from 0.76 to 0.71 under a different model version. Numerous depth and geometric-graph entries change, including o4-mini short BST-depth accuracy from 0.01 to 1.00. Code, parsing, paraphrase, and strategy-selection findings are newly reported.

T1.justification: The data-structure definitions and Levenshtein discussion are substantively retained. Neither version introduces formal theoretical results or proofs; v2's additional motivation and diagnostic explanations do not establish new mathematical claims.

C1.justification: v2 adds a central abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim that models fail to reason reliably over their generated code, with external execution offering limited transfer to nonstandard or natural-language tasks. It also broadens the benchmark's stated role as a unified diagnostic for algorithmic reasoning. The original structural-reasoning limitations remain central.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving memorized code patterns, code-writing failures, brittle language parsing, and median-selection errors on nonuniform spatial data. It removes the BST-depth example supporting entrenched priors while retaining the K-D-heap argument. The earlier explicit limitations about unavailable or costly thought traces and uncovered emerging structures are replaced by broader discussion and strategy-adaptation directions.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents native Structured Output or Instructor support, provides an explicit Stepwise schema, and supplies exact code-mode prompts and API-versus-web-interface details. These improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the existing schema-enforcement procedure. The code and data release links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The positioning expands substantially toward algorithmic understanding, scaling limitations, mechanistic interpretability, and reasoning without external tools. New references include Eberle et al., Bounsi et al., Villalobos et al., and IMO evaluations. A new coding-benchmark discussion adds SWE-bench and Aider, while several earlier application, safety, and spatial-reasoning references are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2; benchmark construction is reorganized into tasks, prompt design, and pipeline; experimental settings are integrated into evaluation. Suite terminology and appendix organization also change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned to distinguish main/challenge coverage and the three extension suites. Figure 2 adds GPT-5 and changes its plotted series and legend. Comparison tables expand, numerous code and diagnostic tables are added, and the document adopts different typography and headers. Figures 3 and 4 are retained.

improvement.justification: The new code controls, parsing checks, paraphrase tests, and spatial error analysis strengthen diagnostic support. However, revised results introduce unresolved inconsistencies: v1's o4-mini BST aggregate of 0.86 accords with its near-zero depth scores, whereas v2 retains 0.86 in Table 1 despite every BST entry in Table 14 being at least 0.97. The broader evidence and reduced numerical consistency leave the net quality change uncertain.
